transcript.content:
This would be amazing if I could see it. I really hope the Moon is visible right now!

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-08-14 14:00 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-08-14T21:00:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 63.367 degrees and its azimuth is 206.962 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 50.94 degrees and its azimuth is 157.604 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 5.95 percent illuminated, 28.172 degrees from the Sun, and 371351.1 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To be perfectly honest: **No, you will not be able to see the Moon with your unaided eyes under these conditions.**

While the Moon is technically "above the horizon," there are three main reasons why it will be invisible to you right now:

### 1. The "Daylight Washout" Effect
You mentioned the sky brightness is "bright daylight" and the Sun is at a very high altitude (63.367 degrees). At this time of day, the atmosphere is saturated with scattered sunlight (Rayleigh scattering). This creates a massive amount of background "noise" in the sky. Because the Moon is only 5.95% illuminated (a very thin crescent), it does not have enough surface area reflecting light to compete with the brilliance of the blue sky.

### 2. The Proximity to the Sun
The Moon is only 28.172 degrees away from the Sun. In astronomical terms, this is very close. Because the Moon is so near the Sun in the sky, it is sitting in the brightest part of the atmosphere. Even if it were a Full Moon, it would be very difficult to see; because it is a tiny sliver (a crescent), it is effectively lost in the glare.

### 3. Contrast
For an object to be visible to the human eye, there must be enough contrast between the object and the background. 
*   **At night:** The background is black, so even a 5% illuminated Moon stands out clearly.
*   **At 2:00 PM:** The background is bright blue/white. A 5% illuminated Moon is simply too dim to provide enough contrast to be distinguished from the surrounding sky.

### Summary
If you look toward the azimuth of **157.6°** (which is roughly **South-Southeast**), you will see a very bright, clear sky. You won't see the Moon, but you are looking in the right direction! 

**Tip:** If you have a pair of **binoculars** or a **telescope**, you might be able to spot it! Optics can help "block out" some of the surrounding sky and magnify the sliver of the Moon, potentially allowing you to see it even in the daytime.
